sets.title: Which fundraiser makes more sense?
sets.summary: Students read a student editorial that uses costs, profit and rates to argue for a fundraiser, and practice reading data, identifying a claim and evaluating evidence.

passage.title: Plant Sale or Car Wash? Let the Numbers Decide
paragraphs: Our seventh-grade class needs to raise money for a trip to the science museum in March. At last week's class meeting, students suggested two fundraisers: a plant sale and a car wash. Both ideas are popular, and both could work. However, before we vote, I believe we should compare the numbers carefully. When I did the math, the plant sale came out as the smarter choice.

For the plant sale, we would buy 60 small vegetable plants from a local farm for $90. We would sell each plant for $4. If we sell all 60 plants, we would collect $240. After we subtract the $90 we spent, our profit would be $150. Mr. Haddad estimates that the sale would need about 15 volunteer hours in total.

For the car wash, supplies such as soap, sponges and buckets would cost about $40. We would charge $8 per car. Last year, a similar car wash at our school washed 30 cars, so we could expect about $240 in sales and a profit of $200. That is $50 more than the plant sale. However, a car wash needs many helpers. Eight students would have to work for five hours each, which adds up to 40 volunteer hours.

Here is the key point. If we divide profit by volunteer hours, the plant sale earns $10 for every hour of work, while the car wash earns only $5 per hour. In other words, the plant sale earns twice as much for each hour students give. Those saved hours could be used to study for exams or to plan the trip itself.

Weather is another risk. A car wash depends on a sunny day. If it rains and only half as many cars arrive, the profit would drop to $80. Plants, on the other hand, can be sold indoors in the school lobby.

Some classmates argue that the car wash is more fun, and that matters. Still, the main purpose of a fundraiser is to raise money efficiently. For these reasons, I urge everyone to vote for the plant sale. Written by Priya N., Grade 7 class representative.

glossary.definition: a chance that something bad could happen

items.stem: Look at the table. How much would the supplies for the car wash cost?

choices.why: $90 is the cost for the plant sale.
choices.misconception: Reads the wrong row of the table

choices.why: $240 is the money collected, not the cost.
choices.misconception: Reads the wrong column of the table

choices.why: The car wash row shows a cost of $40.

items.stem: What would the class sell at the plant sale?

choices.text: fruit
choices.why: The editorial does not say the class would sell fruit.
choices.misconception: Adds information that is not in the text

choices.text: vegetable plants
choices.why: Paragraph 2 says the class would buy and sell 60 small vegetable plants.

choices.text: seed packets
choices.why: Seeds are close, but the text says small plants, not seeds.
choices.misconception: Chooses a related word instead of the exact detail

items.stem: What is the writer's main claim?

choices.text: The class should vote for the plant sale because it earns more money for each hour of work.
choices.why: The writer states this choice in the first and last paragraphs and supports it with rates.

choices.text: The car wash would earn $50 more profit than the plant sale.
choices.why: This is a true detail, but it actually supports the other side.
choices.misconception: Mistakes a supporting detail for the main claim

choices.text: A fundraiser should be fun for everyone.
choices.why: This is the counterargument that the writer answers, not the writer's claim.
choices.misconception: Confuses the counterargument with the claim

choices.text: The class should not go to the science museum.
choices.why: The writer wants to raise money for the museum trip.
choices.misconception: Contradicts the text

items.stem: In paragraph 6, the writer says a fundraiser should raise money "efficiently." What does efficiently mean in this sentence?

choices.text: as fast as possible, no matter how much money is made
choices.why: Speed is only part of the idea; the writer cares about money earned for the work.
choices.misconception: Gives a partial meaning of the word

choices.text: with as much fun as possible
choices.why: Fun is what the other classmates want, which the writer contrasts with efficiency.
choices.misconception: Uses a nearby idea that means something different

choices.text: on the sunniest day of the year
choices.why: Weather is discussed in a different paragraph and is not the meaning of the word.
choices.misconception: Connects the word to an unrelated paragraph

choices.text: without wasting time or work
choices.why: The writer compares money per hour, so efficiently means getting the most from students' work.

items.stem: The writer says rain is a risk. If it rains, the car wash profit drops to $80, but it still takes 40 volunteer hours. How much would the car wash earn for each volunteer hour then?

choices.text: $5 per hour
choices.why: $5 per hour is the rate on a sunny day, not a rainy day.
choices.misconception: Uses the number for a different situation

choices.text: $2 per hour
choices.why: A profit of $80 divided by 40 hours is $2 for each hour.

choices.text: $3 per hour
choices.why: This uses $120 in sales and forgets to subtract the $40 for supplies.
choices.misconception: Confuses money collected with profit

choices.text: $10 per hour
choices.why: $10 per hour is the plant sale rate.
choices.misconception: Uses data from the wrong option

items.stem: Which piece of information, if it were true, would most weaken the writer's argument?

choices.text: The science museum trip is planned for March.
choices.why: The date of the trip does not change which fundraiser earns more.
choices.misconception: Picks a true detail that does not affect the claim

choices.text: Plants can be sold indoors in the school lobby.
choices.why: This helps the writer's argument instead of weakening it.
choices.misconception: Chooses evidence that supports the claim instead of weakening it

choices.text: Most families at the school already grow their own vegetables, so few plants would sell.
choices.why: If few plants sell, the plant sale profit and its money per hour would drop.

choices.text: Some students think a car wash is more fun.
choices.why: The writer already admits this, and it does not change the numbers.
choices.misconception: Repeats a counterargument the writer has already answered

sets.title: Two maps, one neighborhood
sets.summary: Students read an informational text about comparing a 1925 map and a modern map of a neighborhood and practice locating details, explaining causes, stating main ideas and inferring.

passage.title: Reading Old and New Maps of Riverside
paragraphs: Maps do more than show where places are. When historians compare maps from different years, they can see how a community has changed. Last fall, students at Northgate Middle School compared two maps of their own neighborhood, Riverside. One map was drawn in 1925, and the other was printed last year.

On the 1925 map, Riverside looks very different. The river is lined with factories and warehouses, and a railroad runs along the water. Small houses are packed close together on narrow streets near the factories. The map key shows only one school and one park. Most workers walked to their jobs because few families owned cars.

The modern map tells a new story. The railroad tracks along the river have become a walking and biking trail. Two of the old warehouses are now apartment buildings, and another is a public library. The map key shows three schools, four parks and two bus routes. A wide road now connects Riverside to the downtown area.

Why did these changes happen? The students found clues at the local history museum. In the 1960s, many factories closed or moved to places where land was cheaper. Without the factories, the railroad was no longer needed. For years, many buildings stood empty. Then, in the 1990s, residents formed a neighborhood council and asked the city to turn the empty spaces into places that people could use every day.

The students also noticed what stayed the same. The river still curves around the neighborhood in the same shape, and the oldest street, Mill Lane, has the same name it had in 1925. Some families have lived on Mill Lane for four generations.

Comparing maps helped the students understand that a community is not fixed. It changes as jobs, transportation and the needs of residents change. At the end of the project, the class created a third map that shows how they hope Riverside will look in 2050.

items.stem: On the 1925 map, how many schools does the map key show?

choices.text: one
choices.why: Paragraph 2 says the 1925 map key shows only one school.

choices.text: three
choices.why: Three schools are on the modern map, not the 1925 map.
choices.misconception: Uses a detail from the wrong paragraph

choices.text: four
choices.why: Four is the number of parks on the modern map.
choices.misconception: Takes a number that answers a different question

items.stem: What did the old railroad tracks become?

choices.text: a public library
choices.why: An old warehouse became a library, not the railroad tracks.
choices.misconception: Matches the wrong old place with a new place

choices.text: a bus route
choices.why: Bus routes are on the modern map, but the text does not say they replaced the tracks.
choices.misconception: Picks a true detail that does not answer the question

choices.text: a walking and biking trail
choices.why: Paragraph 3 says the railroad tracks became a walking and biking trail.

items.stem: According to paragraph 4, why was the railroad no longer needed?

choices.text: Residents asked the city to build a trail.
choices.why: The trail came later, after the railroad was already unused.
choices.misconception: Reverses cause and effect

choices.text: Most workers walked to their jobs.
choices.why: This is true about 1925, but it is not the reason given in paragraph 4.
choices.misconception: Picks a true detail from the wrong paragraph

choices.text: The river changed its shape.
choices.why: The passage says the river kept the same shape.
choices.misconception: Contradicts a stated fact

choices.text: Many factories closed or moved away.
choices.why: Paragraph 4 says that without the factories, the railroad was no longer needed.

items.stem: Which sentence best states the main idea of the whole passage?

choices.text: Mill Lane is the oldest street in Riverside.
choices.why: This is one detail from one paragraph.
choices.misconception: Chooses a main idea that is too narrow

choices.text: Comparing old and new maps shows how a community changes over time.
choices.why: Every paragraph adds to the idea that the maps reveal change in Riverside.

choices.text: Factories are always bad for neighborhoods.
choices.why: The author does not give this opinion.
choices.misconception: Adds an opinion that is not in the text

choices.text: Every city has a river and a railroad.
choices.why: The passage is about one neighborhood, not every city.
choices.misconception: Overgeneralizes beyond the text

items.stem: What can you infer about the residents who formed the neighborhood council in the 1990s?

choices.text: They wanted the empty buildings and spaces to be useful to the community again.
choices.why: They asked the city to turn empty spaces into places people could use every day.

choices.text: They wanted the factories and the railroad to come back.
choices.why: The empty spaces became a trail, apartments and a library, not factories.
choices.misconception: Draws a conclusion the outcome does not support

choices.text: They all worked in the warehouses in 1925.
choices.why: The council formed about 70 years later, and the text does not say this.
choices.misconception: Confuses the time periods in the text

choices.text: They did not like parks or libraries.
choices.why: The neighborhood gained parks and a library after their request.
choices.misconception: Contradicts the evidence in the text

items.stem: Why does the author include paragraph 5 about what stayed the same?

choices.text: To explain why the factories closed
choices.why: The reasons for the factories closing are in a different paragraph.
choices.misconception: Uses a detail from the wrong paragraph

choices.text: To argue that Mill Lane should get a new name
choices.why: The author points out that the name stayed the same and does not argue for a change.
choices.misconception: Invents an argument the author does not make

choices.text: To show that even a changing community keeps some links to its past
choices.why: The same river shape, street name and long-time families connect Riverside to its history.

choices.text: To teach readers how to draw a map key
choices.why: The passage mentions map keys but never explains how to make one.
choices.misconception: Chooses a purpose the text does not support

sets.title: Signs in a new city
sets.summary: Students read an original short story about a girl and her grandfather in a new city and practice finding details, interpreting figurative language, tracing character change and choosing evidence for a theme.

passage.title: Signs
paragraphs: The first week in our new city, every street sign looked like a locked door to me. I could read the letters, of course. I had studied English for three years. But the words moved too fast past the bus windows, and the names of the streets twisted into shapes I did not recognize.

My grandfather, Grandpa Ilir, could not read the signs at all. Each morning he asked me to walk him to the corner market, and each morning I sighed loudly enough for him to hear. I wanted to stay home and message my friends from our old school, who still felt closer than anyone here.

One rainy Saturday, Grandpa did not wait for me. When I woke up, his coat was gone from its hook. My mother's face went pale. We searched the nearby streets for an hour, calling his name until our voices cracked. At last, we found him at the bus stop on Elm Avenue, holding a soggy paper covered with his own careful drawings.

It was a map. He had drawn the bakery with a small loaf of bread, the library with a book, and the market with an apple. Next to each picture, he had copied the English words from the signs, letter by letter, like a student practicing spelling. Some letters were backward. All of them were neat.

"I did not want to be a heavy bag you must carry," he said quietly. Rain dripped from his hat. I felt something tighten in my chest. I had thought only about what the move had taken from me. I had never imagined how small the city must feel to someone who could not read a single word on its walls.

That evening, we sat at the kitchen table with colored pencils. I wrote the street names in large letters, and Grandpa drew the pictures. By the end of the month, he could read twelve signs by himself. And somehow, the signs had stopped looking like locked doors to me, too.

glossary.definition: to know something because you have seen it before
glossary.esDefinition: saber qué es algo porque ya lo viste antes

glossary.definition: having less color than usual, often from fear
glossary.esDefinition: con menos color de lo normal, muchas veces por miedo

items.stem: Where did the family find Grandpa?

choices.text: at the corner market
choices.why: The market is where he usually went, but he was found somewhere else.
choices.misconception: Picks a place from the text that does not answer the question

choices.text: at the bus stop
choices.why: Paragraph 3 says they found him at the bus stop on Elm Avenue.

choices.text: at the library
choices.why: The library is a place on his drawing, not where they found him.
choices.misconception: Uses a detail from the wrong paragraph

items.stem: What picture did Grandpa draw for the library?

choices.text: a book
choices.why: Paragraph 4 says he drew the library with a book.

choices.text: a loaf of bread
choices.why: The bread was his picture for the bakery.
choices.misconception: Matches a detail to the wrong place

choices.text: an apple
choices.why: The apple was his picture for the market.
choices.misconception: Matches a detail to the wrong place

items.stem: The narrator says every street sign "looked like a locked door." What does this comparison mean?

choices.text: The signs were hung on real doors.
choices.why: The narrator is comparing, not saying the signs were on doors.
choices.misconception: Reads figurative language literally

choices.text: The signs were painted in bright colors.
choices.why: Nothing in the story describes the colors of the signs.
choices.misconception: Adds information that is not in the text

choices.text: The signs were hard for her to understand, so the city felt closed to her.
choices.why: A locked door keeps you out, just as the confusing signs made her feel shut out.

choices.text: The stores were closed on Saturday.
choices.why: The story never says the stores were closed.
choices.misconception: Adds information that is not in the text

items.stem: Why did the narrator's mother's face go pale?

choices.text: Rain was dripping from Grandpa's hat.
choices.why: This happens later, after they find Grandpa.
choices.misconception: Puts events in the wrong order

choices.text: She could not read the street signs.
choices.why: The story says Grandpa could not read the signs, not the mother.
choices.misconception: Gives a detail to the wrong character

choices.text: Grandpa had copied some letters backward.
choices.why: The backward letters are on the map, found later, and do not explain her fear.
choices.misconception: Connects two ideas the text does not connect

choices.text: Grandpa's coat was gone, and no one knew where he was.
choices.why: The pale face comes right after they see his coat is gone, so she was afraid for him.

items.stem: How does the narrator's attitude toward helping Grandpa change during the story?

choices.text: She goes from happy to annoyed.
choices.why: She sighs at the start and helps gladly at the end, so this is backward.
choices.misconception: Reverses the direction of the change

choices.text: She goes from feeling annoyed to wanting to help him become independent.
choices.why: At first she sighs loudly, but at the end she makes signs with him so he can read on his own.

choices.text: She stays bored and annoyed the whole time.
choices.why: The kitchen-table scene shows that her feelings change.
choices.misconception: Ignores the character's change

choices.text: She becomes afraid of the new city.
choices.why: By the end, the city feels less closed to her, not more frightening.
choices.misconception: Misreads the ending

items.stem: A theme of the story is that understanding someone else's struggle can change how we see our own. Which sentence best supports this theme?

choices.text: "I had never imagined how small the city must feel to someone who could not read a single word on its walls."
choices.why: Here the narrator stops thinking only of herself and sees Grandpa's struggle.

choices.text: "One rainy Saturday, Grandpa did not wait for me."
choices.why: This sentence starts an event in the plot but does not show a change in understanding.
choices.misconception: Chooses a plot event instead of evidence for the theme

choices.text: "He had drawn the bakery with a small loaf of bread."
choices.why: This is a detail about the map, not about what the narrator learns.
choices.misconception: Picks a true detail that does not support the claim

choices.text: "I had studied English for three years."
choices.why: This is background information and says nothing about her change.
choices.misconception: Picks a true detail that does not support the claim
